title: Which model for which process: an interactive guide | halilneed
name: Which model for which process
desc: A map from everyday business tasks to the smallest model that does them: rules or a model, six kinds of model, four questions that choose, and where each department can start.
ogDesc: Rules or a model, six kinds of model and four questions that choose. Four interactive steps.
heroP: A map from everyday business tasks to the smallest model that does them.
s1p: The task: spot refund requests. Add words to the rule and see what it misses.
s1cap: The model column is illustrative: what a small classifier trained on examples typically does.
s2p: Tap a kind: what goes in, what comes out, where it works.
note2: Most business steps need a model far smaller than a chat model.
s3p: Answer in order. The first “yes” picks the kind.
note3: If every answer is “no”, you need a generative model. It is the most flexible and the most expensive option.
s4p: Pick your department and see where to begin.
r2: The smallest model that does the job
ctaP: What to mask and what to keep in-house before text reaches a model.

js.shareText: Rules or a model? Six kinds of model and four questions that choose. The smallest right model for your department, in a 15-minute interactive guide:
messages: I want to return my order
Can I get my money back?
The item arrived broken, I want a refund
These shoes don’t fit, what can I do?
I read your return policy, thanks
I’d like to change my billing address
kwLesson: A one-word rule is exact, but it misses requests worded differently. Add words.
Every new word catches something and brings a false alarm. A model learns from examples, and it is sometimes wrong too.
